-\section{Fourth-moment coefficient-calculus example}%
-\label{app:optional-fourth-moment-coefficient-algebra}
-\label{app:fourth-moment-coupling-proof}
-
-The fourth-moment material is not used in the three main theorems.  Its role
-is only to illustrate how the sixth-order coefficient \(A_6\) can be read as
-a simple algebraic defect after normalizing to unit variance.  The proof
-below supplies the elementary coupling estimate underlying the
-fourth-moment discussion; it uses no finite-time KL estimate and no
-eighth-order coefficient.
-
-\begin{lemma}[Normalized fourth-moment defect algebra]%
-\label{lem:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-defect-algebra}
-Let \(X\) be a real random variable with \(\EE X=0\), \(\EE X^2=1\), and
-\(\EE X^4<\infty\).  Put
-\[
-\beta_3=\EE X^3,\qquad
-Q_2=X^2-1-\beta_3X,\qquad
-\kappa=\EE Q_2^2,\qquad
-\eta=\frac{\beta_3^2}{32}+\frac{\kappa}{8}.
-\]
-Then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-algebra}
-\eta
-=\frac{\beta_3^2}{32}+\frac{\EE(X^2-1-\beta_3X)^2}{8}
-=\frac{\EE X^4-1}{8}-\frac{3\beta_3^2}{32}.
-\end{equation}
-In particular \(\eta\ge0\), and \(\eta=0\) if and only if
-\(\mathcal L(X)=\rho_1:=\frac12(\delta_{-1}+\delta_1)\).
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Expanding \(Q_2^2\) and using \(\EE X=0\), \(\EE X^2=1\), and
-\(\EE X^3=\beta_3\) gives
-\[
-\kappa
-=\EE[(X^2-1-\beta_3X)^2]
-=\EE[(X^2-1)^2]-\beta_3^2
-=\EE X^4-1-\beta_3^2.
-\]
-Substitution gives \eqref{eq:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-algebra}.
-The first displayed form of \(\eta\) proves non-negativity.  If
-\(\eta=0\), then \(\beta_3=0\) and \(Q_2=0\) almost surely, hence
-\(X^2=1\) almost surely; since \(\EE X=0\), the two signs have equal mass.
-The converse is immediate.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{lemma}[Elementary normalized \(W_2\) coupling]%
-\label{lem:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-w2-coupling}
-Let \(X\) be a real random variable with \(\EE X=0\), \(\EE X^2=1\), and
-\(\EE X^4<\infty\), and define \(\eta\) as in
-Lemma~\ref{lem:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-defect-algebra}.  Then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:appendix-normalized-sign-rademacher-coupling}
-W_2(\mathcal L(X),\rho_1)
-\le 4\eta^{1/4}+8\eta^{1/2}.
-\end{equation}
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Let
-\[
-M:=\EE[(X^2-1)^2].
-\]
-The calculation in the preceding lemma gives
-\[
-M=\kappa+\beta_3^2\le32\eta .
-\]
-Let \(S=1\) on \(\{X\ge0\}\) and \(S=-1\) on \(\{X<0\}\), and write
-\(r_p=\mathcal L(S)=p\delta_1+(1-p)\delta_{-1}\).  For every real \(x\),
-with this convention at \(x=0\),
-\[
-|x-\operatorname{sgn}x|\le |x^2-1|.
-\]
-Indeed \(|x^2-1|=|x-1|(x+1)\) for \(x\ge0\), and
-\(|x^2-1|=|x+1|(1-x)\) for \(x<0\).  Coupling \(X\) and \(S\) on the same
-probability space gives
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:appendix-couple-x-to-sign}
-W_2(\mathcal L(X),r_p)
-\le \bigl(\EE|X-S|^2\bigr)^{1/2}
-\le M^{1/2}.
-\end{equation}
-
-It remains to couple the biased sign law to the symmetric Rademacher law.
-On the two-point set \(\{-1,1\}\), optimal quadratic transport moves the
-excess mass \(|p-\frac12|\) across distance \(2\), so
-\[
-W_2(r_p,\rho_1)^2=4\left|p-\frac12\right|.
-\]
-Since \(\EE X=0\),
-\[
-2p-1=\EE S=\EE(S-X),
-\]
-and Cauchy--Schwarz together with
-\eqref{eq:appendix-couple-x-to-sign} gives
-\[
-\left|p-\frac12\right|
-\le \frac12\EE|S-X|
-\le \frac12 M^{1/2}.
-\]
-Consequently
-\[
-W_2(r_p,\rho_1)\le \sqrt2\,M^{1/4}.
-\]
-The triangle inequality now yields
-\[
-W_2(\mathcal L(X),\rho_1)
-\le M^{1/2}+\sqrt2\,M^{1/4}
-\le \sqrt{32}\,\eta^{1/2}+\sqrt2\,32^{1/4}\eta^{1/4}.
-\]
-Since \(\sqrt{32}<8\) and \(\sqrt2\,32^{1/4}=2^{7/4}<4\), this proves
-\eqref{eq:appendix-normalized-sign-rademacher-coupling}.
-\end{proof}
-
-For a law \(\nu\) with mean \(\bar\gamma\) and variance \(\sigma^2>0\), set
-\(X=(\gamma-\bar\gamma)/\sigma\), let
-\(\nu_c=(\gamma-\bar\gamma)_\#\nu\), and put
-\(\rho_\sigma=\frac12(\delta_{-\sigma}+\delta_\sigma)\).  Quadratic
-Wasserstein distance is homogeneous under dilation:
-\[
-W_2\bigl((x\mapsto ax)_\#\mu,(x\mapsto ax)_\#\rho\bigr)
-=|a|\,W_2(\mu,\rho).
-\]
-Define
-\[
-\Delta_6(\nu)
-:=\sigma^6\left(
-\frac{\beta_3^2}{32}+\frac{\EE(X^2-1-\beta_3X)^2}{8}
-\right).
-\]
-Combining this dilation identity with the normalized lemma gives exactly the
-estimate used in the main text,
-\[
-W_2(\nu_c,\rho_\sigma)
-\le
-4\,\sigma^{-1/2}\Delta_6(\nu)^{1/4}
-+8\,\sigma^{-2}\Delta_6(\nu)^{1/2},
-\]
-Equality \(\Delta_6(\nu)=0\) is equivalent to the symmetric two-point centred
-law.  Thus the appendix supplies a self-contained algebraic coupling proof,
-not an additional finite-time stability theorem.
-
-\section{Weighted trigonometric normalization}%
-\label{app:entropy-integrals}
-\label{app:background-symbol-criterion}
-
-This appendix records the change of variables behind the Laurent coefficient
-normalization.  Set \(y=\tan\theta\),
-\(-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2\).  Then
-\[
-  \frac{\dd y}{\pi(1+y^2)}=\frac{\dd\theta}{\pi}.
-\]
-With \(z=e^{2\ii\theta}\),
-\[
-  \cos(2k\theta)=\frac{z^k+z^{-k}}2,\qquad
-  \sin(2k\theta)=\frac{z^k-z^{-k}}{2\ii}.
-\]
-Thus the Cauchy mode integrals in
-Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-fourier-mode-integral-algorithm} are exactly Haar
-constant terms:
-\[
-  \int_{\RR}\prod_j u_{n_j}(y)\,\omega(\dd y)
-  =[z^0]\prod_j Q_{n_j}(z).
-\]
-For order eight, Appendix~\ref{app:order-eight-laurent-certificate} records
-the row certificate as a finite coefficient-calculus check.
-

-For \(0<\alpha<2\), let \(p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\) be the density of any
-centred isotropic strictly \(\alpha\)-stable law on \(\RR^d\), and use the
-spatial-scale normalization
-\[
- p_s^{(\alpha,d)}(x)=s^{-d}p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(x/s),\qquad s>0.
-\]
-Changing the scale parameter in the characteristic exponent only changes
-the choice of \(p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\), so this notation covers every isotropic
-strictly stable kernel.  Put
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-critical-exponents}
- \beta=d+\alpha,\qquad
- q_{\alpha,d}:=\min\left\{2,1+\frac4\beta\right\},\qquad
- p_{\alpha,d}:=\frac4{q_{\alpha,d}}
- =\max\left\{2,\frac{4(d+\alpha)}{d+\alpha+4}\right\}.
-\end{equation}
-Write \(\Omega_{\alpha,d}(\dd y)=p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)\dd y\) and
-\[
-F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)
-:=\frac{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y-z)}{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}.
-\]
-
-\begin{proposition}[Stable-kernel input package]
-\label{prop:stable-kernel-input-package}
-Put \(\beta=d+\alpha\).  For every multi-index \(\gamma\), there are positive
-constants \(c,C,C_\gamma\), depending on \(d,\alpha\) and the chosen stable
-scale, such that
-\begin{align}
- c(1+|y|)^{-\beta}&\le p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)
- \le C(1+|y|)^{-\beta},\label{eq:stable-input-density}\\
- |\partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)|
- &\le C_\gamma(1+|y|)^{-\beta-|\gamma|},\label{eq:stable-input-derivative}\\
- \frac{|\partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)|}
- {p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}
- &\le C_\gamma(1+|y|)^{-|\gamma|}.
- \label{eq:stable-input-derivative-quotient}
-\end{align}
-In particular, \(p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\) is strictly positive and smooth,
-\(\|\nabla\log p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\|_\infty<\infty\), and
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-input-translation-continuity}
- \|\partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(\mathord\cdot-z)
-       -\partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\|_1\longrightarrow0
- \qquad(z\to0).
-\end{equation}
-If the characteristic exponent is changed from \(|\xi|^\alpha\) to
-\(a|\xi|^\alpha\), put \(\lambda=a^{1/\alpha}\).  The new unit-scale density
-is \(p_{1,a}(y)=\lambda^{-d}p_1(y/\lambda)\).  Thus the density bound has
-factor \(\lambda^{-d}\), the derivative bound has factor
-\(\lambda^{-d-|\gamma|}\), and the quotient bound has factor
-\(\lambda^{-|\gamma|}\), with \(1+|y|\) replaced throughout by
-\(1+|y|/\lambda\).  Equivalently, all later
-constants are locally uniform when \(a\) ranges in a compact subset of
-\((0,\infty)\).
-\end{proposition}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Properties (G)(i)--(iii) of \cite{IshigeKawakamiMichihisa2017}, also recorded
-in the refined formulation of
-\cite{IshigeKawakamiMichihisa2022RefinedFractional}, give strict positivity,
-smoothness, the derivative upper bounds, and the positive tail asymptotic
-\(p_1(y)\asymp |y|^{-d-\alpha}\) outside a sufficiently large ball.  The
-tail asymptotic supplies the lower bound in
-\eqref{eq:stable-input-density} there.  On the remaining compact ball,
-strict positivity and continuity give a positive minimum; enlarging the
-upper constant completes the global two-sided density bound.  Dividing
-\eqref{eq:stable-input-derivative} by this lower bound proves
-\eqref{eq:stable-input-derivative-quotient}, including the log-gradient
-bound.  The derivative estimate makes every \(\partial^\gamma p_1\)
-integrable, so ordinary \(L^1\)-translation continuity gives
-\eqref{eq:stable-input-translation-continuity}.  The assertions about \(a\)
-follow directly by differentiating the displayed dilation formula.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{lemma}[Stable critical translation remainder]
-\label{lem:stable-critical-translation-remainder}
-Let \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha<2\), \(p=p_{\alpha,d}\),
-\(q=q_{\alpha,d}\), and \(m=\lfloor p\rfloor\).  If
-\(T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(y,z)\) is the Taylor polynomial of
-\(F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\) at \(z=0\) through degree \(m\), then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-translation-lq-growth}
- c_{\alpha,d,q}(1+|z|)^{\beta(q-1)}
- \le \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}^q
- \le C_{\alpha,d,q}(1+|z|)^{\beta(q-1)}.
-\end{equation}
-Moreover,
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-critical-global-remainder}
- \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,z)\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}
- \le C_{\alpha,d}
- \begin{cases}
-  |z|^{m+1},&|z|\le1,\\
-  |z|^p,&|z|>1,
- \end{cases}
- \le C_{\alpha,d}|z|^p.
-\end{equation}
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package} supplies all density,
-derivative, quotient, and translation estimates used below.  The upper
-bound in \eqref{eq:stable-translation-lq-growth} follows from
-\[
- \begin{aligned}
- \int p_1(y-z)^q p_1(y)^{1-q}\dd y
- &\le C\int(1+|y-z|)^{-\beta q}
-              (1+|y|)^{\beta(q-1)}\dd y\\
- &\le C(1+|z|)^{\beta(q-1)}
-       \int(1+|y-z|)^{-\beta}\dd y,
- \end{aligned}
-\]
-where \(p_1=p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\) and
-\(1+|y|\le(1+|z|)(1+|y-z|)\).  The final integral is finite because
-\(\beta>d\).  For the lower bound, integrate over \(|y-z|\le1\) and use
-\eqref{eq:stable-input-density}; this gives the claimed power
-for \(|z|\ge2\).  Positivity and continuity on bounded \(z\)-sets complete
-the estimate.
-
-For \(|z|\le1\), Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package} also gives
-\(p_1(y-\theta z)\le C p_1(y)\), uniformly in \(0\le\theta\le1\).
-Taylor's formula along the segment from \(y\) to \(y-z\), followed by the
-derivative bound in \eqref{eq:stable-input-derivative}, therefore
-gives the pointwise bound
-\(|F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(y,z)|\le C|z|^{m+1}\), uniformly
-in \(y\).  For \(|z|>1\), \eqref{eq:stable-translation-lq-growth} gives
-\(\|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\|_q\le C|z|^{\beta(1-1/q)}\).  The Taylor
-coefficients are bounded, so
-\(\|T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,z)\|_q\le C|z|^m\).  Finally,
-\[
- \beta(1-1/q)\le p,\qquad m\le p<m+1,
-\]
-with equality in the first relation when \(\beta>4\).  These observations
-prove \eqref{eq:stable-critical-global-remainder}.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{lemma}[Critical Bregman perturbation bound]
-\label{lem:critical-lq-kl-perturbation}
-Let \(1<q\le2\) and
-\(\Phi(s)=(1+s)\log(1+s)-s\) on \([-1,\infty)\), with
-\(0\log0=0\).  There is a constant \(C_q\) such that
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-bregman-pointwise-bound}
- 0\le \Phi(u+v)-\Phi(u)-\log(1+u)v\le C_q|v|^q
-\end{equation}
-whenever \(|u|\le1/4\) and \(u+v\ge-1\).
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-The lower bound is convexity.  If \(|v|\le1/2\), the segment between
-\(u\) and \(u+v\) is contained in \([-3/4,3/4]\).  Since
-\(\Phi''(s)=(1+s)^{-1}\) there, Taylor's theorem gives an upper bound
-\(C v^2\le C|v|^q\).  If \(v<-1/2\), the admissible pairs
-\((u,v)\) range over a compact set and \(|v|^q\ge2^{-q}\); continuity at
-\(u+v=-1\) gives the result.  If \(v>1/2\), direct expansion of the left
-side shows that it is at most \(C(1+v)\log(1+v)+Cv\), which is bounded by
-\(C_qv^q\).  These three regions prove
-\eqref{eq:critical-bregman-pointwise-bound}.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{theorem}[Optimal uniform sufficient moment exponent for stable KL asymptotics]
-\label{thm:high-dimensional-kl-moment-threshold}
-Let \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha<2\), and let \(\nu\) be a probability law on
-\(\RR^d\) with mean \(\bar\gamma\).  Put
-\(X=\gamma-\bar\gamma\), and assume
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-kl-moment-hypothesis}
- \EE|X|^{p_{\alpha,d}}<\infty,
- \qquad
- p_{\alpha,d}=\max\left\{2,
- \frac{4(d+\alpha)}{d+\alpha+4}\right\},
-\end{equation}
-then the covariance \(\Sigma=\EE[XX^{\mathsf T}]\) is finite and
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-kl-leading-asymptotic}
- H_{\alpha,d}(s):=
- D_{\rm KL}\!\left(p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu\,\middle\|\,
- p_s^{(\alpha,d)}(\mathord\cdot-\bar\gamma)\right)
- =\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)s^{-4}+o(s^{-4}),
-\end{equation}
-where
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-leading-covariance-functional}
- b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}(y)
- :=\frac1{2p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}
-   \sum_{i,j=1}^d\Sigma_{ij}\partial_{ij}p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y),
- \qquad
- \mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)
- :=\frac12\int b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}^2\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}.
-\end{equation}
-The exponent is optimal only in the following uniform sense.  For every
-\(0<r<2\), there is a mean-zero law with finite \(r\)th absolute moment
-and \(\limsup_{s\to\infty}s^4H_{\alpha,d}(s)=+\infty\).  If
-\(d+\alpha>4\), then for every \(2\le r<p_{\alpha,d}\) the counterexample
-may additionally be chosen with positive-definite finite covariance.
-Thus no smaller moment exponent implies
-\eqref{eq:critical-kl-leading-asymptotic} uniformly over its entire moment
-class, and the endpoint belongs to the sufficient side.
-
-This is not a law-by-law moment criterion.  When \(d+\alpha>4\), finite
-\(p_{\alpha,d}\)-moment is not asserted to be necessary for an individual
-law; the exact finite-covariance criterion is the nonlinear raw-tail energy
-in Theorem~\ref{thm:stable-law-by-law-decomposition} below.  When
-\(d+\alpha\le4\), the exponent is two and boundedness of
-\(s^4H_{\alpha,d}(s)\) does force finite covariance, as the proof below
-shows.  For \(\alpha=1\) with the standard normalization
-\(p_1^{(1,d)}=P_1^{(d)}\), one has
-\(\mathcal Q_{1,d}=\mathcal Q_d\), so the theorem contains the radial
-Poisson result above.
-\end{theorem}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Translation permits us to assume \(\bar\gamma=0\).  Fix
-\(q=q_{\alpha,d}\), \(p=p_{\alpha,d}\), and \(m=\lfloor p\rfloor\),
-and write
-\[
- R_m(y,z)=F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(y,z),
- \qquad r_s(y)=\EE R_m(y,X/s).
-\]
-Minkowski's inequality and
-\eqref{eq:stable-critical-global-remainder} give
-\[
- s^p\|R_m(\cdot,X/s)\|_q\le C_{\alpha,d}|X|^p.
-\]
-For each fixed \(X\), the local part of the same estimate and \(m+1>p\)
-give
-\[
- s^p\|R_m(\cdot,X/s)\|_q
- \le C_{\alpha,d}|X|^{m+1}s^{p-m-1}\longrightarrow0.
-\]
-Dominated convergence therefore yields
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-lq-integrated-remainder}
- \|r_s\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}=o(s^{-p}).
-\end{equation}
-
-Centering removes the linear Taylor layer.  Averaging the remaining layers
-gives
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-kl-quotient-decomposition}
- \delta_s^{(\alpha,d)}=u_s+r_s,
- \qquad
- u_s=s^{-2}b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}
-       +\mathbf 1_{\{m=3\}}s^{-3}B_3,
-\end{equation}
-where \(B_3\) is a bounded linear combination of third-order modes.  In the
-second case the required third moments exist because \(p\ge3\).  Hence
-\(\|u_s\|_\infty=O(s^{-2})\).  The boundedness of all these modes follows
-from Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package}.
-
-The identity
-\(F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\Omega_{\alpha,d}(\dd y)
-=p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y-z)\dd y\) shows that every translated quotient has
-integral one.  Moreover,
-\(\int|F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-1|\Omega_{\alpha,d}(\dd y)\le2\), so Tonelli's
-theorem gives \(\delta_s^{(\alpha,d)}\in L^1(\Omega_{\alpha,d})\) with
-zero integral.  The KL change of variables is therefore
-\[
- H_{\alpha,d}(s)=\int\Phi(\delta_s^{(\alpha,d)})\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}
-\]
-in the extended sense.  For all sufficiently large \(s\), apply
-Lemma~\ref{lem:critical-lq-kl-perturbation} to \(u=u_s\), \(v=r_s\).
-Hölder's inequality and \eqref{eq:critical-lq-integrated-remainder} give
-\begin{align*}
- \left|H_{\alpha,d}(s)-\int\Phi(u_s)\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}\right|
- &\le \|\log(1+u_s)\|_{q/(q-1)}\|r_s\|_q
-       +C_q\|r_s\|_q^q\\
- &\le O(s^{-2})o(s^{-p})+o(s^{-pq})=o(s^{-4}),
-\end{align*}
-because \(p\ge2\) and \(pq=4\).
-This estimate also proves that the extended KL integral is finite for all
-sufficiently large \(s\).
-
-Finally, the boundedness of the retained modes permits a uniform Taylor
-expansion of \(\Phi(u_s)\).  From
-\eqref{eq:critical-kl-quotient-decomposition},
-\[
- \int\Phi(u_s)\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}
- =\frac{s^{-4}}2\int b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}^2\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}
-   +o(s^{-4})
- =\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)s^{-4}+o(s^{-4}),
-\]
-which proves \eqref{eq:critical-kl-leading-asymptotic}.
-
-We first prove the obstruction below two moments.  If
-\(\limsup_{s\to\infty}s^4H_{\alpha,d}(s)<\infty\), Pinsker's inequality
-and scaling give, for every fixed \(\xi\in\RR^d\),
-\[
- |\widehat p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(\xi)|
- |\varphi_X(\xi/s)-1|
- \le \|p_1^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu_s-p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\|_1
- \le \sqrt{2H_{\alpha,d}(s)}=O(s^{-2}),
-\]
-where \(\nu_s\) is the law of \(X/s\).  Since the stable characteristic
-function never vanishes, take \(\xi=e\) for a unit vector \(e\), multiply
-the real part by \(s^2\), and use Fatou's lemma to obtain
-\[
- \frac12\EE(e\cdot X)^2
- \le \liminf_{s\to\infty}s^2
-       \EE[1-\cos((e\cdot X)/s)]<\infty.
-\]
-Thus bounded scaled entropy forces finite covariance.  Given \(0<r<2\),
-choose \(a\in(\max\{1,r\},2)\) and put symmetric masses proportional to
-\(n^{-a-1}\) at \(\pm ne_1\), with the remaining mass at zero.  This law
-has mean zero and finite \(r\)th moment but infinite variance, so its scaled
-entropy has infinite limsup.
-
-It remains to prove optimality between two and \(p\) when \(\beta>4\).
-Fix \(2\le r<p\), choose positive \(a_j\) with \(\sum_ja_j<\infty\), and
-put symmetric masses \(w_j/2\) at \(\pm R_je_1\), where
-\(w_j=a_jR_j^{-r}\).  Add a sufficiently small bounded symmetric spanning
-component.  The resulting law has positive-definite finite covariance and
-finite \(r\)th moment.  Set
-\[
- s_j=\kappa R_jw_j^{1/\beta},\qquad
- A_j=B(R_je_1,s_j).
-\]
-The component at \(R_je_1\) gives
-\((p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu)(A_j)\ge c_{\alpha,d}w_j\).  On the other hand,
-\eqref{eq:stable-input-density} and \(s_j/R_j\to0\) give
-\[
- p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}(A_j)
- \le C_{\alpha,d}(s_j/R_j)^\beta
- =C_{\alpha,d}\kappa^\beta w_j.
-\]
-Choose \(\kappa\) so that
-\(C_{\alpha,d}\kappa^\beta<c_{\alpha,d}\).  Data processing to
-\(\{A_j,A_j^c\}\) and
-Lemma~\ref{lem:bernoulli-kl-linear-separation} then yield
-\(H_{\alpha,d}(s_j)\ge c w_j\), and hence
-\[
- s_j^4H_{\alpha,d}(s_j)
- \ge cR_j^4w_j^{1+4/\beta}
- =ca_j^{q_{\alpha,d}}R_j^{4-rq_{\alpha,d}}.
-\]
-Here \(q_{\alpha,d}=1+4/\beta\) and
-\(r<p=4/q_{\alpha,d}\), so the exponent of \(R_j\) is positive.
-Recursive choice of the radii makes \(s_j\to\infty\) and the last display
-unbounded while preserving all moment assertions.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{lemma}[All-order stable critical remainder]
-\label{lem:all-order-stable-critical-remainder}
-Let \(r\ge1\), put \(\beta=d+\alpha\), and define
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-critical-exponents}
- q_{r,\alpha,d}:=\min\left\{2,1+\frac{2r}{d+\alpha}\right\},
- \qquad
- p_{r,\alpha,d}:=\frac{2r}{q_{r,\alpha,d}}
- =\max\left\{r,\frac{2r(d+\alpha)}{d+\alpha+2r}\right\}.
-\end{equation}
-Let \(q=q_{r,\alpha,d}\), \(p=p_{r,\alpha,d}\), and
-\(m=\lfloor p\rfloor\).  If \(T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(y,z)\) is the Taylor
-polynomial of \(F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\) at zero through degree \(m\), then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-critical-remainder}
- \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,z)\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}
- \le C_{\alpha,d,r}
- \begin{cases}
-  |z|^{m+1},&|z|\le1,\\
-  |z|^p,&|z|>1,
- \end{cases}
- \le C_{\alpha,d,r}|z|^p.
-\end{equation}
-Consequently, if a probability law \(\lambda\) on \(\RR^d\) has finite
-\(p\)th absolute moment and
-\[
- q_s^\lambda(y):=\int F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(x/s)\lambda(\dd x),
-\]
-then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-integrated-remainder}
- q_s^\lambda
- =1+\sum_{j=1}^m s^{-j}B_j^\lambda+r_s^\lambda,
- \qquad
- \|r_s^\lambda\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}=o(s^{-p}),
-\end{equation}
-where
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-moment-modes}
- B_j^\lambda(y):=
- \frac{(-1)^j}{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}
- \sum_{|\gamma|=j}\frac{m_\gamma(\lambda)}{\gamma!}
- \partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y),
- \qquad
- m_\gamma(\lambda):=\int x^\gamma\lambda(\dd x).
-\end{equation}
-Every \(B_j^\lambda\) in this display is bounded.
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-The proof of \eqref{eq:stable-translation-lq-growth} applies verbatim for
-every fixed \(1<q\le2\) and gives
-\[
- \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}
- \le C(1+|z|)^{\beta(1-1/q)}.
-\]
-The local Taylor argument in the proof of
-Lemma~\ref{lem:stable-critical-translation-remainder} gives the first line
-of \eqref{eq:all-order-stable-critical-remainder}.  For \(|z|>1\), the
-Taylor modes are bounded by
-Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package}, and
-hence
-\[
- \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,z)\|_q
- \le C\{|z|^{\beta(1-1/q)}+|z|^m\}\le C|z|^p.
-\]
-Indeed, \(m\le p\), while
-\(\beta(1-1/q)\le p\); in the non-Hilbert regime
-\(\beta>2r\), both sides of the latter inequality equal
-\(2r\beta/(\beta+2r)\).  Since \(m+1>p\), the final inequality in
-\eqref{eq:all-order-stable-critical-remainder} also holds on the unit ball.
-
-Taylor's formula gives \eqref{eq:all-order-stable-integrated-remainder}
-before its norm assertion.  For fixed \(x\), the local estimate implies
-\[
- s^p\|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(x/s)
-       -T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,x/s)\|_q\longrightarrow0,
-\]
-whereas \eqref{eq:all-order-stable-critical-remainder} bounds this expression
-by \(C|x|^p\).  Minkowski's inequality and dominated convergence prove the
-claimed \(L^q\) remainder.  Boundedness of the modes follows again from
-Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package}.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{lemma}[Two-background critical Bregman transfer]
-\label{lem:two-background-critical-bregman-transfer}
-Let \(1<q\le2\), \(p\ge r>0\), and \(pq=2r\).  On a probability space
-\((E,\Omega)\), suppose \(g_s\ge c_s>0\),
-\[
- \int g_s\dd\Omega=1,\qquad c_s\longrightarrow1,
- \qquad \|g_s-1\|_{L^1(\Omega)}\longrightarrow0.
-\]
-Let \(B\in L^\infty(\Omega)\), and suppose
-\[
- v_s=s^{-r}B+o(s^{-r})\quad\hbox{in }L^\infty(\Omega),
- \qquad \|e_s\|_{L^q(\Omega)}=o(s^{-p}).
-\]
-If \(g_s+v_s+e_s\ge0\) and both \(g_s\Omega\) and
-\((g_s+v_s+e_s)\Omega\) are probability measures, then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-background-critical-bregman-transfer}
- D_{\rm KL}((g_s+v_s+e_s)\Omega\|g_s\Omega)
- =\frac{s^{-2r}}2\int B^2\dd\Omega+o(s^{-2r}).
-\end{equation}
-\end{lemma}
-
-The hypotheses on the denominator in this lemma deliberately stop short of
-\(L^\infty\)-convergence to one.  They require only a positive lower bound
-approaching one, mass normalization, and \(L^1\)-convergence.  This weaker
-interface is what permits a heavy-tailed translated mixture to serve as the
-background.
-
-\begin{proof}
-For \(g>0\), write \(\Psi_g(z)=g\Phi(z/g)\).  Scaling
-Lemma~\ref{lem:critical-lq-kl-perturbation} shows, whenever
-\(|v/g|\le1/4\) and \(g+v+e\ge0\), that
-\[
- 0\le\Psi_g(v+e)-\Psi_g(v)
-      -\log(1+v/g)e\le C_q g^{1-q}|e|^q.
-\]
-For large \(s\), the hypotheses give \(g_s\ge1/2\) and
-\(\|v_s/g_s\|_\infty\le1/4\).  Therefore H\"older's inequality yields
-\begin{align*}
- &\left|D_{\rm KL}((g_s+v_s+e_s)\Omega\|g_s\Omega)
-       -\int\Psi_{g_s}(v_s)\dd\Omega\right|\\
- &\qquad\le
- C\|v_s\|_{L^{q/(q-1)}}\|e_s\|_{L^q}
- +C\|e_s\|_{L^q}^q
- =o(s^{-r-p})+o(s^{-pq})=o(s^{-2r}).
-\end{align*}
-Uniform Taylor expansion at zero gives
-\[
- \int\Psi_{g_s}(v_s)\dd\Omega
- =\frac12\int\frac{v_s^2}{g_s}\dd\Omega+O(\|v_s\|_\infty^3).
-\]
-Finally,
-\[
- \left|\int B^2(g_s^{-1}-1)\dd\Omega\right|
- \le2\|B\|_\infty^2\|g_s-1\|_1\longrightarrow0,
-\]
-and \eqref{eq:two-background-critical-bregman-transfer} follows.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{lemma}[Finite-difference moment blocks]
-\label{lem:stable-finite-difference-blocks}
-Let \(r\ge1\), let \(e\) be a unit vector, and define
-\[
- \sigma_R:=2^{1-r}\sum_{k=0}^r(-1)^{r-k}\binom rk
-                 \delta_{(k+1)Re}=A_R^+-A_R^-.
-\]
-Then \(A_R^+\) and \(A_R^-\) are probability measures and
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-block-moment-identities}
- \int x^\gamma\dd\sigma_R(x)=0\quad(|\gamma|<r),
- \qquad
- \int(e\cdot x)^r\dd\sigma_R(x)=2^{1-r}r!R^r.
-\end{equation}
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-The positive and negative binomial coefficients each sum to \(2^{r-1}\),
-and the order-\(r\) forward-difference identity gives
-\eqref{eq:stable-block-moment-identities}.  In particular, when \(r=1\),
-\(\sigma_R=\delta_{2Re}-\delta_{Re}\); the same cancellation and nonzero
-first-difference conclusions hold without a separate construction.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{lemma}[Moving-ball probability separation]
-\label{lem:stable-moving-ball-probability-separation}
-Let \(\beta=d+\alpha\), let \(A_R^\pm\) be the blocks in
-Lemma~\ref{lem:stable-finite-difference-blocks}, and suppose
-\[
- R_{j+1}>4(r+1)R_j,
- \qquad w_j>0,
- \qquad \sum_jw_j<1.
-\]
-Define
-\[
- \nu=\left(1-\sum_jw_j\right)\delta_0+\sum_jw_jA_{R_j}^+,
- \qquad
- \eta=\left(1-\sum_jw_j\right)\delta_0+\sum_jw_jA_{R_j}^-.
-\]
-Put \(x_j=(r+1)R_je\), choose
-\(s_j=\kappa R_jw_j^{1/\beta}<R_j/4\), and set
-\(E_j=B(x_j,s_j)\).  There are constants \(a_r>0\) and
-\(C_{\alpha,d,r}<\infty\), independent of \(j,\kappa,R_j,w_j\), such that
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-moving-ball-probability-separation}
- (p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu)(E_j)\ge a_rw_j,
- \qquad
- (p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}*\eta)(E_j)
- \le C_{\alpha,d,r}\kappa^\beta w_j.
-\end{equation}
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-The endpoint coefficient in \(A_{R_j}^+\) at \(x_j\) is \(2^{1-r}\).
-Stable scaling and positivity therefore give
-\[
- (p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu)(E_j)
- \ge 2^{1-r}w_j\int_{B(0,1)}p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)\dd y
- =:a_rw_j.
-\]
-We verify the separation from every atom of \(\eta\).  In block \(j\),
-opposite-sign atoms are at least \(R_j\) from \(x_j\).  Every earlier atom
-has norm at most \((r+1)R_{j-1}<R_j/4\), whereas every later atom has norm at
-least \(R_{j+1}>4(r+1)R_j\); the atom at zero obeys the earlier-atom bound.
-After subtracting the radius \(s_j<R_j/4\), every such atom \(z\) satisfies
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-moving-ball-distance}
- \operatorname{dist}(z,E_j)\ge3R_j/4.
-\end{equation}
-For \(y\in E_j\), the stable density upper bound and scaling now give
-\[
- p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}(y-z)
- \le C_{\alpha,d,r}s_j^\alpha R_j^{-\beta}.

-\label{thm:low-dimensional-finite-covariance-threshold}
-Let \(1\le d\le3\), and let \(\nu\) be a probability law on \(\RR^d\) with
-finite mean.  With
-\[
- H_d(t)=D_{\rm KL}\!\left(P_t^{(d)}*\nu\,\middle\|\,
- P_t^{(d)}(\mathord\cdot-\bar\gamma)\right),
-\]
-one has
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:low-dimensional-covariance-iff}
- \EE|X|^2<\infty
- \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
- \limsup_{t\to\infty}t^4H_d(t)<\infty.
-\end{equation}
-If the covariance is finite, then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:low-dimensional-covariance-limit}
- H_d(t)=\mathcal Q_d(\Sigma)t^{-4}+o(t^{-4}).
-\end{equation}
-If it is infinite, then \(t^4H_d(t)\to+\infty\) in the extended sense.
-\end{theorem}
-
-\begin{proof}
-For \(d\le3\), \(q_d=2\).  Thus Theorem
-\ref{thm:multidim-l2-moment-threshold} and the \(L^2\) alternative in
-Theorem~\ref{thm:second-order-quotient-kl-coefficient} prove
-\eqref{eq:low-dimensional-covariance-limit}.  The entropy representation is
-valid in the extended sense by change of variables; for large \(t\), the
-\(L^2\) convergence makes \(\Phi(\delta_t^{(d)})\) integrable because
-\(\Phi(s)\le C s^2\) on \([-1,\infty)\).
-
-Conversely, if \(\EE|X|^2=\infty\), some unit vector \(e\) satisfies
-\(\EE(e\cdot X)^2=\infty\).  Projection onto \(e\) sends the radial
-\(d\)-dimensional Poisson law to the one-dimensional Cauchy law at the same
-scale.  The data-processing inequality and
-Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp-leading-kl-variance-threshold} therefore give
-\[
- H_d(t)\ge
- D_{\rm KL}(P_t*\nu_e\|P_t(\mathord\cdot-\bar\gamma_e)),
-\]
-whose product with \(t^4\) tends to \(+\infty\).
-\end{proof}

-\begin{proposition}[Finite covariance does not control high-dimensional KL]
-\label{prop:high-dimensional-finite-covariance-obstruction}
-For every \(d\ge4\), there exists a centred discrete probability law on
-\(\RR^d\) with positive-definite finite covariance such that
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:high-dimensional-finite-covariance-obstruction}
- \limsup_{t\to\infty}t^4H_d(t)=+\infty.
-\end{equation}
-\end{proposition}

-\begin{proof}
-Choose positive \(\alpha_j\) with \(\sum_j\alpha_j<\infty\), radii
-\(R_j\uparrow\infty\), and weights
-\(w_j=\alpha_jR_j^{-2}\).  After rescaling the sequence if necessary,
-\(W=\sum_jw_j<1\).  Begin with
-\[
- (1-W)\delta_0+\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{w_j}{2}
- (\delta_{R_je_1}+\delta_{-R_je_1}),
-\]
-and transfer an arbitrarily small amount of the mass at zero to a bounded
-centred symmetric law spanning \(\RR^d\).  The covariance is then positive
-definite and finite because \(\sum_jw_jR_j^2=\sum_j\alpha_j<\infty\).
-
-Fix a sufficiently small constant \(\kappa>0\), and set
-\[
- t_j=\kappa R_jw_j^{1/(d+1)}.
-\]
-The radii may be chosen recursively so that \(t_j\to\infty\).  Let \(A_j\)
-be the ball of radius \(t_j\) centred at \(R_je_1\).  The \(j\)th mixture
-component gives
-\[
- (P_{t_j}^{(d)}*\nu)(A_j)\ge c_dw_j,
-\]
-whereas, since \(t_j/R_j\to0\), the centred reference satisfies
-\[
- P_{t_j}^{(d)}(A_j)
- \le C_d(t_j/R_j)^{d+1}
- =C_d\kappa^{d+1}w_j.
-\]
-Choose \(\kappa\) so that the second constant is strictly smaller than the
-first.  Data processing to the partition \(\{A_j,A_j^c\}\) and
-Lemma~\ref{lem:bernoulli-kl-linear-separation} then give
-\(H_d(t_j)\ge c'_dw_j\).  Hence
-\[
- t_j^4H_d(t_j)
- \ge c''_dR_j^4w_j^{1+4/(d+1)}
- =c''_d\alpha_j^{1+4/(d+1)}
- R_j^{2(d-3)/(d+1)}.
-\]
-The exponent of \(R_j\) is positive exactly when \(d>3\).  Choosing the
-radii recursively makes the final expression tend to infinity.
-\end{proof}
-
-For the high-dimensional entropy topology, define
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-kl-exponents}
- q_d:=\frac{d+5}{d+1},
- \qquad
- p_d:=\frac{4(d+1)}{d+5}.
-\end{equation}
-Thus \(1<q_d<2\), \(2<p_d<4\), and \(p_dq_d=4\) when \(d\ge4\).
-
-\begin{lemma}[Critical translation remainder]
-\label{lem:critical-lq-translation-remainder}
-Let \(d\ge4\), let \(p_d,q_d\) be as in
-\eqref{eq:critical-kl-exponents}, and put \(m=\lfloor p_d\rfloor\).
-If \(T_m(y,z)\) is the Taylor polynomial of \(F_y(z)\) through degree
-\(m\), then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-lq-exact-translation-norm}
- \|F_\cdot(z)\|_{L^{q_d}(\Omega_d)}^{q_d}
- =1+\frac{2(d+5)}{(d+1)(d+3)}|z|^2
- +\frac{3}{(d+1)(d+3)}|z|^4.
-\end{equation}
-Consequently, for a constant depending only on \(d\),
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-lq-global-remainder}
- \|F_\cdot(z)-T_m(\cdot,z)\|_{L^{q_d}(\Omega_d)}
- \le C_d
- \begin{cases}
- |z|^{m+1},& |z|\le1,\\
- |z|^{p_d},& |z|>1,
- \end{cases}
- \le C_d|z|^{p_d}.
-\end{equation}
-Here \(m=2\) for \(4\le d\le10\), while \(m=3\) for \(d\ge11\),
-including the integer endpoint \(p_{11}=3\).
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Since \(a(q_d-1)=2\), translation by \(z\) gives
-\[
- \|F_\cdot(z)\|_{q_d}^{q_d}
- =c_d\int_{\RR^d}
- \frac{(1+|u+z|^2)^2}{(1+|u|^2)^{(d+5)/2}}\dd u.
-\]
-Write \(A=1+|u|^2\).  The odd term in the expansion of
-\((A+|z|^2+2u\cdot z)^2\) integrates to zero, and rotational invariance
-gives
-\[
- \int(u\cdot z)^2(1+|u|^2)^{-(d+5)/2}\dd u
- =\frac{|z|^2}{d}\int |u|^2(1+|u|^2)^{-(d+5)/2}\dd u.
-\]
-The three normalized beta integrals needed here are
-\[
- \begin{aligned}
- c_d\int(1+|u|^2)^{-(d+1)/2}\dd u&=1,\\
- c_d\int(1+|u|^2)^{-(d+3)/2}\dd u&=\frac1{d+1},\\
- c_d\int(1+|u|^2)^{-(d+5)/2}\dd u
- &=\frac3{(d+1)(d+3)}.
- \end{aligned}
-\]
-Substitution proves \eqref{eq:critical-lq-exact-translation-norm}.
-
-For \(|z|\le1\), the local quotient--Taylor estimate
-\eqref{eq:local-multidim-taylor-remainder} implies the first line of
-\eqref{eq:critical-lq-global-remainder}.  For \(|z|>1\), the exact identity
-gives \(\|F_\cdot(z)\|_{q_d}\le C_d|z|^{4/q_d}=C_d|z|^{p_d}\).
-Every coefficient of \(T_m\) is bounded in \(y\), and \(m\le p_d\), so
-\(\|T_m(\cdot,z)\|_{q_d}\le C_d|z|^{p_d}\).  Finally,
-\(m+1>p_d\), which proves the last inequality for \(|z|\le1\).
-\end{proof}

-\section{Related-work comparison}%
-\label{app:related-work-scope}
-
-This appendix separates the theorem statements in the paper from nearby
-results that use similar words--entropy, transport, Poisson, heat profile,
-or Hardy--Stein--for different objects.  The introduction organizes the
-closest comparisons by mathematical mechanism.  The longer table below
-records additional entropy, Sobolev--Bregman, heat-profile,
-Poisson-channel papers, Cauchy-divergence formulas, and general
-entropy-representation references.  The distinctions used in the table are
-structural: the present law \(\nu\) is fixed, the reference is the
-mean-matched harmonic Poisson/Cauchy kernel, and the coefficients are obtained
-by expanding the quotient before applying
-\(\Phi(s)=(1+s)\log(1+s)-s\).

-
-Closed formulas for divergences between Cauchy laws also do not imply the
-coefficient hierarchy above.  Results such as Nielsen--Okamura
-\cite{NielsenOkamura2023Cauchy}, Nielsen
-\cite{Nielsen2020CauchyVoronoi}, and Verd{\'u}
-\cite{Verdu2023Cauchy} evaluate \(f\)-divergences or information-geometric
-quantities when both arguments are members of a finite-dimensional Cauchy
-family.  In the present problem the numerator \(P_t*\nu\) is generally a
-mixture of Cauchy translates, not a single Cauchy law; only the denominator is
-the mean-matched Cauchy kernel.  Even when a law is approximated by a nearby
-Cauchy profile, the KL coefficients are not obtained by differentiating the
-two-parameter Cauchy divergence formula: after centering, the linear term in
-the quotient integrates to zero, while the \(t^{-2m}\) coefficient collects
-all products of quotient modes whose total order is \(2m\) through the
-nonlinear series for \(\Phi\).  The fixed-law hierarchy is therefore a
-moment-polynomial constant-term calculation for a Cauchy mixture quotient,
-not an expansion inside the Cauchy statistical manifold.
-
-The regularly varying boundary theorem uses Karamata theory in a different
-role from stable-limit entropy theory.  The integrated slow-variation facts
-and direct/tail integral theorems are classical
-\cite{BinghamGoldieTeugels1987RegularVariation}; they identify the truncated
-moment and control the local and far parts of the Cayley quotient.  Entropic
-convergence to stable laws and stable de Bruijn or fractional-information
-identities
-\cite{BobkovChistyakovGotze2013StableEntropy,Johnson2013StableDeBruijn,
-Toscani2016StableEntropy} instead concern normalized convolution sequences,
-stable interpolation, or entropy dissipation relative to a stable target.
-They do not give the coefficient-subtracted, moving-Cauchy-reference
-asymptotic of
-Theorem~\ref{cor:main-body-conditional-missing-top-moment-tail}.  The new
-step is the distribution-level \(L^\infty\cap L^1(\omega)\) quotient jet at
-the exact divergent moment boundary and its transfer to the signed
-\(t^{-2N}\ell_L(t)\) residual.  Karamata's theorem itself is cited as an
-external input and is not reproved here.
-
-The Poisson terminology also hides adjacent but different entropy theories.
-Poisson-channel papers such as Guo--Shamai--Verd{\'u}
-\cite{GuoShamaiVerdu2008PoissonChannel} and Atar--Weissman
-\cite{AtarWeissman2012PoissonChannel} study conditional count outputs
-\(Y|X\sim{\rm Poisson}(\gamma X)\) or continuous-time counting processes and
-relate mutual information, relative entropy, and estimation loss.  These are
-count-output models rather than harmonic smoothing by \(P_t\), so they do not
-produce the quotient expansion used in Theorems~\ref{thm:main-A}
-and~\ref{thm:main-B}.
-
-Small-time heat-kernel entropy expansions have a different limiting regime.
-For example, the expansions of
-Menkovski--Portegies--Ravelonanosy
-\cite{MenkovskiPortegiesRavelonanosy2024HeatKernelEntropy} treat the
-relative entropy between a heat kernel and normalized Riemannian volume as the
-heat time tends to zero; the coefficients are universal local geometric
-invariants of the underlying manifold.  By contrast, here \(t\to\infty\), the
-underlying space is Euclidean, the reference is the translated harmonic
-Poisson/Cauchy kernel \(P_t(\cdot-\bar\gamma)\), and the coefficients depend
-on the fixed input law only through its centred moments and the Cayley Laurent
-constant-term rule.  Process and discretization entropy asymptotics, such as
-Fageot--Fallah--Horel
-\cite{FageotFallahHorel2022EntropicCompressibilityLevy} and
-Ghourchian--Amini--Gohari
-\cite{GhourchianAminiGohari2018InnovationCompressibility}, concern
-compressibility or innovation limits rather than a single fixed law smoothed
-by a harmonic semigroup.  General representation formulas, including the
-Gibbs--Donsker--Varadhan variational formula
-\cite{DonskerVaradhan1975AsymptoticI,DupuisEllis1997WeakConvergence} and
-semigroup de Bruijn identities such as
-\cite{DeBruijn1953,HirataNemotoYoshida2012IntegralRepresentation,
-Yoshida2017RelativeEntropyDiffusion}, identify entropy through optimization
-or dissipation.  They are structural identities, not coefficient evaluations
-for the matched large-\(t\) functional in
-\eqref{eq:intro-main-functional}.

-\section{Fourth-moment coefficient-calculus example}%
-\label{app:optional-fourth-moment-coefficient-algebra}
-\label{app:fourth-moment-coupling-proof}
-
-The fourth-moment material is not used in the three main theorems.  Its role
-is only to illustrate how the sixth-order coefficient \(A_6\) can be read as
-a simple algebraic defect after normalizing to unit variance.  The proof
-below supplies the elementary coupling estimate underlying the
-fourth-moment discussion; it uses no finite-time KL estimate and no
-eighth-order coefficient.
-
-\begin{lemma}[Normalized fourth-moment defect algebra]%
-\label{lem:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-defect-algebra}
-Let \(X\) be a real random variable with \(\EE X=0\), \(\EE X^2=1\), and
-\(\EE X^4<\infty\).  Put
-\[
-\beta_3=\EE X^3,\qquad
-Q_2=X^2-1-\beta_3X,\qquad
-\kappa=\EE Q_2^2,\qquad
-\eta=\frac{\beta_3^2}{32}+\frac{\kappa}{8}.
-\]
-Then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-algebra}
-\eta
-=\frac{\beta_3^2}{32}+\frac{\EE(X^2-1-\beta_3X)^2}{8}
-=\frac{\EE X^4-1}{8}-\frac{3\beta_3^2}{32}.
-\end{equation}
-In particular \(\eta\ge0\), and \(\eta=0\) if and only if
-\(\mathcal L(X)=\rho_1:=\frac12(\delta_{-1}+\delta_1)\).
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Expanding \(Q_2^2\) and using \(\EE X=0\), \(\EE X^2=1\), and
-\(\EE X^3=\beta_3\) gives
-\[
-\kappa
-=\EE[(X^2-1-\beta_3X)^2]
-=\EE[(X^2-1)^2]-\beta_3^2
-=\EE X^4-1-\beta_3^2.
-\]
-Substitution gives \eqref{eq:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-algebra}.
-The first displayed form of \(\eta\) proves non-negativity.  If
-\(\eta=0\), then \(\beta_3=0\) and \(Q_2=0\) almost surely, hence
-\(X^2=1\) almost surely; since \(\EE X=0\), the two signs have equal mass.
-The converse is immediate.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{lemma}[Elementary normalized \(W_2\) coupling]%
-\label{lem:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-w2-coupling}
-Let \(X\) be a real random variable with \(\EE X=0\), \(\EE X^2=1\), and
-\(\EE X^4<\infty\), and define \(\eta\) as in
-Lemma~\ref{lem:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-defect-algebra}.  Then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:appendix-normalized-sign-rademacher-coupling}
-W_2(\mathcal L(X),\rho_1)
-\le 4\eta^{1/4}+8\eta^{1/2}.
-\end{equation}
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Let
-\[
-M:=\EE[(X^2-1)^2].
-\]
-The calculation in the preceding lemma gives
-\[
-M=\kappa+\beta_3^2\le32\eta .
-\]
-Let \(S=1\) on \(\{X\ge0\}\) and \(S=-1\) on \(\{X<0\}\), and write
-\(r_p=\mathcal L(S)=p\delta_1+(1-p)\delta_{-1}\).  For every real \(x\),
-with this convention at \(x=0\),
-\[
-|x-\operatorname{sgn}x|\le |x^2-1|.
-\]
-Indeed \(|x^2-1|=|x-1|(x+1)\) for \(x\ge0\), and
-\(|x^2-1|=|x+1|(1-x)\) for \(x<0\).  Coupling \(X\) and \(S\) on the same
-probability space gives
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:appendix-couple-x-to-sign}
-W_2(\mathcal L(X),r_p)
-\le \bigl(\EE|X-S|^2\bigr)^{1/2}
-\le M^{1/2}.
-\end{equation}
-
-It remains to couple the biased sign law to the symmetric Rademacher law.
-On the two-point set \(\{-1,1\}\), optimal quadratic transport moves the
-excess mass \(|p-\frac12|\) across distance \(2\), so
-\[
-W_2(r_p,\rho_1)^2=4\left|p-\frac12\right|.
-\]
-Since \(\EE X=0\),
-\[
-2p-1=\EE S=\EE(S-X),
-\]
-and Cauchy--Schwarz together with
-\eqref{eq:appendix-couple-x-to-sign} gives
-\[
-\left|p-\frac12\right|
-\le \frac12\EE|S-X|
-\le \frac12 M^{1/2}.
-\]
-Consequently
-\[
-W_2(r_p,\rho_1)\le \sqrt2\,M^{1/4}.
-\]
-The triangle inequality now yields
-\[
-W_2(\mathcal L(X),\rho_1)
-\le M^{1/2}+\sqrt2\,M^{1/4}
-\le \sqrt{32}\,\eta^{1/2}+\sqrt2\,32^{1/4}\eta^{1/4}.
-\]
-Since \(\sqrt{32}<8\) and \(\sqrt2\,32^{1/4}=2^{7/4}<4\), this proves
-\eqref{eq:appendix-normalized-sign-rademacher-coupling}.
-\end{proof}
-
-For a law \(\nu\) with mean \(\bar\gamma\) and variance \(\sigma^2>0\), set
-\(X=(\gamma-\bar\gamma)/\sigma\), let
-\(\nu_c=(\gamma-\bar\gamma)_\#\nu\), and put
-\(\rho_\sigma=\frac12(\delta_{-\sigma}+\delta_\sigma)\).  Quadratic
-Wasserstein distance is homogeneous under dilation:
-\[
-W_2\bigl((x\mapsto ax)_\#\mu,(x\mapsto ax)_\#\rho\bigr)
-=|a|\,W_2(\mu,\rho).
-\]
-Define
-\[
-\Delta_6(\nu)
-:=\sigma^6\left(
-\frac{\beta_3^2}{32}+\frac{\EE(X^2-1-\beta_3X)^2}{8}
-\right).
-\]
-Combining this dilation identity with the normalized lemma gives exactly the
-estimate used in the main text,
-\[
-W_2(\nu_c,\rho_\sigma)
-\le
-4\,\sigma^{-1/2}\Delta_6(\nu)^{1/4}
-+8\,\sigma^{-2}\Delta_6(\nu)^{1/2},
-\]
-Equality \(\Delta_6(\nu)=0\) is equivalent to the symmetric two-point centred
-law.  Thus the appendix supplies a self-contained algebraic coupling proof,
-not an additional finite-time stability theorem.
-
-\section{Weighted trigonometric normalization}%
-\label{app:entropy-integrals}
-\label{app:background-symbol-criterion}
-
-This appendix records the change of variables behind the Laurent coefficient
-normalization.  Set \(y=\tan\theta\),
-\(-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2\).  Then
-\[
-  \frac{\dd y}{\pi(1+y^2)}=\frac{\dd\theta}{\pi}.
-\]
-With \(z=e^{2\ii\theta}\),
-\[
-  \cos(2k\theta)=\frac{z^k+z^{-k}}2,\qquad
-  \sin(2k\theta)=\frac{z^k-z^{-k}}{2\ii}.
-\]
-Thus the Cauchy mode integrals in
-Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-fourier-mode-integral-algorithm} are exactly Haar
-constant terms:
-\[
-  \int_{\RR}\prod_j u_{n_j}(y)\,\omega(\dd y)
-  =[z^0]\prod_j Q_{n_j}(z).
-\]
-For order eight, Appendix~\ref{app:order-eight-laurent-certificate} records
-the row certificate as a finite coefficient-calculus check.
-

-For \(0<\alpha<2\), let \(p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\) be the density of any
-centred isotropic strictly \(\alpha\)-stable law on \(\RR^d\), and use the
-spatial-scale normalization
-\[
- p_s^{(\alpha,d)}(x)=s^{-d}p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(x/s),\qquad s>0.
-\]
-Changing the scale parameter in the characteristic exponent only changes
-the choice of \(p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\), so this notation covers every isotropic
-strictly stable kernel.  Put
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-critical-exponents}
- \beta=d+\alpha,\qquad
- q_{\alpha,d}:=\min\left\{2,1+\frac4\beta\right\},\qquad
- p_{\alpha,d}:=\frac4{q_{\alpha,d}}
- =\max\left\{2,\frac{4(d+\alpha)}{d+\alpha+4}\right\}.
-\end{equation}
-Write \(\Omega_{\alpha,d}(\dd y)=p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)\dd y\) and
-\[
-F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)
-:=\frac{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y-z)}{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}.
-\]

-\begin{proposition}[Stable-kernel input package]
-\label{prop:stable-kernel-input-package}
-Put \(\beta=d+\alpha\).  For every multi-index \(\gamma\), there are positive
-constants \(c,C,C_\gamma\), depending on \(d,\alpha\) and the chosen stable
-scale, such that
-\begin{align}
- c(1+|y|)^{-\beta}&\le p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)
- \le C(1+|y|)^{-\beta},\label{eq:stable-input-density}\\
- |\partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)|
- &\le C_\gamma(1+|y|)^{-\beta-|\gamma|},\label{eq:stable-input-derivative}\\
- \frac{|\partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)|}
- {p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}
- &\le C_\gamma(1+|y|)^{-|\gamma|}.
- \label{eq:stable-input-derivative-quotient}
-\end{align}
-In particular, \(p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\) is strictly positive and smooth,
-\(\|\nabla\log p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\|_\infty<\infty\), and
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-input-translation-continuity}
- \|\partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(\mathord\cdot-z)
-       -\partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\|_1\longrightarrow0
- \qquad(z\to0).
-\end{equation}
-If the characteristic exponent is changed from \(|\xi|^\alpha\) to
-\(a|\xi|^\alpha\), put \(\lambda=a^{1/\alpha}\).  The new unit-scale density
-is \(p_{1,a}(y)=\lambda^{-d}p_1(y/\lambda)\).  Thus the density bound has
-factor \(\lambda^{-d}\), the derivative bound has factor
-\(\lambda^{-d-|\gamma|}\), and the quotient bound has factor
-\(\lambda^{-|\gamma|}\), with \(1+|y|\) replaced throughout by
-\(1+|y|/\lambda\).  Equivalently, all later
-constants are locally uniform when \(a\) ranges in a compact subset of
-\((0,\infty)\).
-\end{proposition}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Properties (G)(i)--(iii) of \cite{IshigeKawakamiMichihisa2017}, also recorded
-in the refined formulation of
-\cite{IshigeKawakamiMichihisa2022RefinedFractional}, give strict positivity,
-smoothness, the derivative upper bounds, and the positive tail asymptotic
-\(p_1(y)\asymp |y|^{-d-\alpha}\) outside a sufficiently large ball.  The
-tail asymptotic supplies the lower bound in
-\eqref{eq:stable-input-density} there.  On the remaining compact ball,
-strict positivity and continuity give a positive minimum; enlarging the
-upper constant completes the global two-sided density bound.  Dividing
-\eqref{eq:stable-input-derivative} by this lower bound proves
-\eqref{eq:stable-input-derivative-quotient}, including the log-gradient
-bound.  The derivative estimate makes every \(\partial^\gamma p_1\)
-integrable, so ordinary \(L^1\)-translation continuity gives
-\eqref{eq:stable-input-translation-continuity}.  The assertions about \(a\)
-follow directly by differentiating the displayed dilation formula.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{lemma}[Stable critical translation remainder]
-\label{lem:stable-critical-translation-remainder}
-Let \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha<2\), \(p=p_{\alpha,d}\),
-\(q=q_{\alpha,d}\), and \(m=\lfloor p\rfloor\).  If
-\(T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(y,z)\) is the Taylor polynomial of
-\(F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\) at \(z=0\) through degree \(m\), then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-translation-lq-growth}
- c_{\alpha,d,q}(1+|z|)^{\beta(q-1)}
- \le \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}^q
- \le C_{\alpha,d,q}(1+|z|)^{\beta(q-1)}.
-\end{equation}
-Moreover,
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-critical-global-remainder}
- \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,z)\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}
- \le C_{\alpha,d}
- \begin{cases}
-  |z|^{m+1},&|z|\le1,\\
-  |z|^p,&|z|>1,
- \end{cases}
- \le C_{\alpha,d}|z|^p.
-\end{equation}
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package} supplies all density,
-derivative, quotient, and translation estimates used below.  The upper
-bound in \eqref{eq:stable-translation-lq-growth} follows from
-\[
- \begin{aligned}
- \int p_1(y-z)^q p_1(y)^{1-q}\dd y
- &\le C\int(1+|y-z|)^{-\beta q}
-              (1+|y|)^{\beta(q-1)}\dd y\\
- &\le C(1+|z|)^{\beta(q-1)}
-       \int(1+|y-z|)^{-\beta}\dd y,
- \end{aligned}
-\]
-where \(p_1=p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\) and
-\(1+|y|\le(1+|z|)(1+|y-z|)\).  The final integral is finite because
-\(\beta>d\).  For the lower bound, integrate over \(|y-z|\le1\) and use
-\eqref{eq:stable-input-density}; this gives the claimed power
-for \(|z|\ge2\).  Positivity and continuity on bounded \(z\)-sets complete
-the estimate.
-
-For \(|z|\le1\), Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package} also gives
-\(p_1(y-\theta z)\le C p_1(y)\), uniformly in \(0\le\theta\le1\).
-Taylor's formula along the segment from \(y\) to \(y-z\), followed by the
-derivative bound in \eqref{eq:stable-input-derivative}, therefore
-gives the pointwise bound
-\(|F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(y,z)|\le C|z|^{m+1}\), uniformly
-in \(y\).  For \(|z|>1\), \eqref{eq:stable-translation-lq-growth} gives
-\(\|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\|_q\le C|z|^{\beta(1-1/q)}\).  The Taylor
-coefficients are bounded, so
-\(\|T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,z)\|_q\le C|z|^m\).  Finally,
-\[
- \beta(1-1/q)\le p,\qquad m\le p<m+1,
-\]
-with equality in the first relation when \(\beta>4\).  These observations
-prove \eqref{eq:stable-critical-global-remainder}.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{lemma}[Critical Bregman perturbation bound]
-\label{lem:critical-lq-kl-perturbation}
-Let \(1<q\le2\) and
-\(\Phi(s)=(1+s)\log(1+s)-s\) on \([-1,\infty)\), with
-\(0\log0=0\).  There is a constant \(C_q\) such that
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-bregman-pointwise-bound}
- 0\le \Phi(u+v)-\Phi(u)-\log(1+u)v\le C_q|v|^q
-\end{equation}
-whenever \(|u|\le1/4\) and \(u+v\ge-1\).
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-The lower bound is convexity.  If \(|v|\le1/2\), the segment between
-\(u\) and \(u+v\) is contained in \([-3/4,3/4]\).  Since
-\(\Phi''(s)=(1+s)^{-1}\) there, Taylor's theorem gives an upper bound
-\(C v^2\le C|v|^q\).  If \(v<-1/2\), the admissible pairs
-\((u,v)\) range over a compact set and \(|v|^q\ge2^{-q}\); continuity at
-\(u+v=-1\) gives the result.  If \(v>1/2\), direct expansion of the left
-side shows that it is at most \(C(1+v)\log(1+v)+Cv\), which is bounded by
-\(C_qv^q\).  These three regions prove
-\eqref{eq:critical-bregman-pointwise-bound}.
-\end{proof}

-\begin{theorem}[Optimal uniform sufficient moment exponent for stable KL asymptotics]
-\label{thm:high-dimensional-kl-moment-threshold}
-Let \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha<2\), and let \(\nu\) be a probability law on
-\(\RR^d\) with mean \(\bar\gamma\).  Put
-\(X=\gamma-\bar\gamma\), and assume
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-kl-moment-hypothesis}
- \EE|X|^{p_{\alpha,d}}<\infty,
- \qquad
- p_{\alpha,d}=\max\left\{2,
- \frac{4(d+\alpha)}{d+\alpha+4}\right\},
-\end{equation}
-then the covariance \(\Sigma=\EE[XX^{\mathsf T}]\) is finite and
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-kl-leading-asymptotic}
- H_{\alpha,d}(s):=
- D_{\rm KL}\!\left(p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu\,\middle\|\,
- p_s^{(\alpha,d)}(\mathord\cdot-\bar\gamma)\right)
- =\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)s^{-4}+o(s^{-4}),
-\end{equation}
-where
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-leading-covariance-functional}
- b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}(y)
- :=\frac1{2p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}
-   \sum_{i,j=1}^d\Sigma_{ij}\partial_{ij}p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y),
- \qquad
- \mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)
- :=\frac12\int b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}^2\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}.
-\end{equation}
-The exponent is optimal only in the following uniform sense.  For every
-\(0<r<2\), there is a mean-zero law with finite \(r\)th absolute moment
-and \(\limsup_{s\to\infty}s^4H_{\alpha,d}(s)=+\infty\).  If
-\(d+\alpha>4\), then for every \(2\le r<p_{\alpha,d}\) the counterexample
-may additionally be chosen with positive-definite finite covariance.
-Thus no smaller moment exponent implies
-\eqref{eq:critical-kl-leading-asymptotic} uniformly over its entire moment
-class, and the endpoint belongs to the sufficient side.
-
-This is not a law-by-law moment criterion.  When \(d+\alpha>4\), finite
-\(p_{\alpha,d}\)-moment is not asserted to be necessary for an individual
-law; the exact finite-covariance criterion is the nonlinear raw-tail energy
-in Theorem~\ref{thm:stable-law-by-law-decomposition} below.  When
-\(d+\alpha\le4\), the exponent is two and boundedness of
-\(s^4H_{\alpha,d}(s)\) does force finite covariance, as the proof below
-shows.  For \(\alpha=1\) with the standard normalization
-\(p_1^{(1,d)}=P_1^{(d)}\), one has
-\(\mathcal Q_{1,d}=\mathcal Q_d\), so the theorem contains the radial
-Poisson result above.
-\end{theorem}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Translation permits us to assume \(\bar\gamma=0\).  Fix
-\(q=q_{\alpha,d}\), \(p=p_{\alpha,d}\), and \(m=\lfloor p\rfloor\),
-and write
-\[
- R_m(y,z)=F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(y,z),
- \qquad r_s(y)=\EE R_m(y,X/s).
-\]
-Minkowski's inequality and
-\eqref{eq:stable-critical-global-remainder} give
-\[
- s^p\|R_m(\cdot,X/s)\|_q\le C_{\alpha,d}|X|^p.
-\]
-For each fixed \(X\), the local part of the same estimate and \(m+1>p\)
-give
-\[
- s^p\|R_m(\cdot,X/s)\|_q
- \le C_{\alpha,d}|X|^{m+1}s^{p-m-1}\longrightarrow0.
-\]
-Dominated convergence therefore yields
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-lq-integrated-remainder}
- \|r_s\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}=o(s^{-p}).
-\end{equation}
-
-Centering removes the linear Taylor layer.  Averaging the remaining layers
-gives
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-kl-quotient-decomposition}
- \delta_s^{(\alpha,d)}=u_s+r_s,
- \qquad
- u_s=s^{-2}b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}
-       +\mathbf 1_{\{m=3\}}s^{-3}B_3,
-\end{equation}
-where \(B_3\) is a bounded linear combination of third-order modes.  In the
-second case the required third moments exist because \(p\ge3\).  Hence
-\(\|u_s\|_\infty=O(s^{-2})\).  The boundedness of all these modes follows
-from Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package}.
-
-The identity
-\(F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\Omega_{\alpha,d}(\dd y)
-=p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y-z)\dd y\) shows that every translated quotient has
-integral one.  Moreover,
-\(\int|F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-1|\Omega_{\alpha,d}(\dd y)\le2\), so Tonelli's
-theorem gives \(\delta_s^{(\alpha,d)}\in L^1(\Omega_{\alpha,d})\) with
-zero integral.  The KL change of variables is therefore
-\[
- H_{\alpha,d}(s)=\int\Phi(\delta_s^{(\alpha,d)})\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}
-\]
-in the extended sense.  For all sufficiently large \(s\), apply
-Lemma~\ref{lem:critical-lq-kl-perturbation} to \(u=u_s\), \(v=r_s\).
-Hölder's inequality and \eqref{eq:critical-lq-integrated-remainder} give
-\begin{align*}
- \left|H_{\alpha,d}(s)-\int\Phi(u_s)\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}\right|
- &\le \|\log(1+u_s)\|_{q/(q-1)}\|r_s\|_q
-       +C_q\|r_s\|_q^q\\
- &\le O(s^{-2})o(s^{-p})+o(s^{-pq})=o(s^{-4}),
-\end{align*}
-because \(p\ge2\) and \(pq=4\).
-This estimate also proves that the extended KL integral is finite for all
-sufficiently large \(s\).
-
-Finally, the boundedness of the retained modes permits a uniform Taylor
-expansion of \(\Phi(u_s)\).  From
-\eqref{eq:critical-kl-quotient-decomposition},
-\[
- \int\Phi(u_s)\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}
- =\frac{s^{-4}}2\int b_{\alpha,d,\Sigma}^2\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}
-   +o(s^{-4})
- =\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)s^{-4}+o(s^{-4}),
-\]
-which proves \eqref{eq:critical-kl-leading-asymptotic}.
-
-We first prove the obstruction below two moments.  If
-\(\limsup_{s\to\infty}s^4H_{\alpha,d}(s)<\infty\), Pinsker's inequality
-and scaling give, for every fixed \(\xi\in\RR^d\),
-\[
- |\widehat p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(\xi)|
- |\varphi_X(\xi/s)-1|
- \le \|p_1^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu_s-p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\|_1
- \le \sqrt{2H_{\alpha,d}(s)}=O(s^{-2}),
-\]
-where \(\nu_s\) is the law of \(X/s\).  Since the stable characteristic
-function never vanishes, take \(\xi=e\) for a unit vector \(e\), multiply
-the real part by \(s^2\), and use Fatou's lemma to obtain
-\[
- \frac12\EE(e\cdot X)^2
- \le \liminf_{s\to\infty}s^2
-       \EE[1-\cos((e\cdot X)/s)]<\infty.
-\]
-Thus bounded scaled entropy forces finite covariance.  Given \(0<r<2\),
-choose \(a\in(\max\{1,r\},2)\) and put symmetric masses proportional to
-\(n^{-a-1}\) at \(\pm ne_1\), with the remaining mass at zero.  This law
-has mean zero and finite \(r\)th moment but infinite variance, so its scaled
-entropy has infinite limsup.
-
-It remains to prove optimality between two and \(p\) when \(\beta>4\).
-Fix \(2\le r<p\), choose positive \(a_j\) with \(\sum_ja_j<\infty\), and
-put symmetric masses \(w_j/2\) at \(\pm R_je_1\), where
-\(w_j=a_jR_j^{-r}\).  Add a sufficiently small bounded symmetric spanning
-component.  The resulting law has positive-definite finite covariance and
-finite \(r\)th moment.  Set
-\[
- s_j=\kappa R_jw_j^{1/\beta},\qquad
- A_j=B(R_je_1,s_j).
-\]
-The component at \(R_je_1\) gives
-\((p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu)(A_j)\ge c_{\alpha,d}w_j\).  On the other hand,
-\eqref{eq:stable-input-density} and \(s_j/R_j\to0\) give
-\[
- p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}(A_j)
- \le C_{\alpha,d}(s_j/R_j)^\beta
- =C_{\alpha,d}\kappa^\beta w_j.
-\]
-Choose \(\kappa\) so that
-\(C_{\alpha,d}\kappa^\beta<c_{\alpha,d}\).  Data processing to
-\(\{A_j,A_j^c\}\) and
-Lemma~\ref{lem:bernoulli-kl-linear-separation} then yield
-\(H_{\alpha,d}(s_j)\ge c w_j\), and hence
-\[
- s_j^4H_{\alpha,d}(s_j)
- \ge cR_j^4w_j^{1+4/\beta}
- =ca_j^{q_{\alpha,d}}R_j^{4-rq_{\alpha,d}}.
-\]
-Here \(q_{\alpha,d}=1+4/\beta\) and
-\(r<p=4/q_{\alpha,d}\), so the exponent of \(R_j\) is positive.
-Recursive choice of the radii makes \(s_j\to\infty\) and the last display
-unbounded while preserving all moment assertions.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{lemma}[All-order stable critical remainder]
-\label{lem:all-order-stable-critical-remainder}
-Let \(r\ge1\), put \(\beta=d+\alpha\), and define
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-critical-exponents}
- q_{r,\alpha,d}:=\min\left\{2,1+\frac{2r}{d+\alpha}\right\},
- \qquad
- p_{r,\alpha,d}:=\frac{2r}{q_{r,\alpha,d}}
- =\max\left\{r,\frac{2r(d+\alpha)}{d+\alpha+2r}\right\}.
-\end{equation}
-Let \(q=q_{r,\alpha,d}\), \(p=p_{r,\alpha,d}\), and
-\(m=\lfloor p\rfloor\).  If \(T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(y,z)\) is the Taylor
-polynomial of \(F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\) at zero through degree \(m\), then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-critical-remainder}
- \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,z)\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}
- \le C_{\alpha,d,r}
- \begin{cases}
-  |z|^{m+1},&|z|\le1,\\
-  |z|^p,&|z|>1,
- \end{cases}
- \le C_{\alpha,d,r}|z|^p.
-\end{equation}
-Consequently, if a probability law \(\lambda\) on \(\RR^d\) has finite
-\(p\)th absolute moment and
-\[
- q_s^\lambda(y):=\int F_y^{(\alpha,d)}(x/s)\lambda(\dd x),
-\]
-then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-integrated-remainder}
- q_s^\lambda
- =1+\sum_{j=1}^m s^{-j}B_j^\lambda+r_s^\lambda,
- \qquad
- \|r_s^\lambda\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}=o(s^{-p}),
-\end{equation}
-where
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:all-order-stable-moment-modes}
- B_j^\lambda(y):=
- \frac{(-1)^j}{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}
- \sum_{|\gamma|=j}\frac{m_\gamma(\lambda)}{\gamma!}
- \partial^\gamma p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y),
- \qquad
- m_\gamma(\lambda):=\int x^\gamma\lambda(\dd x).
-\end{equation}
-Every \(B_j^\lambda\) in this display is bounded.
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-The proof of \eqref{eq:stable-translation-lq-growth} applies verbatim for
-every fixed \(1<q\le2\) and gives
-\[
- \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)\|_{L^q(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}
- \le C(1+|z|)^{\beta(1-1/q)}.
-\]
-The local Taylor argument in the proof of
-Lemma~\ref{lem:stable-critical-translation-remainder} gives the first line
-of \eqref{eq:all-order-stable-critical-remainder}.  For \(|z|>1\), the
-Taylor modes are bounded by
-Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package}, and
-hence
-\[
- \|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(z)-T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,z)\|_q
- \le C\{|z|^{\beta(1-1/q)}+|z|^m\}\le C|z|^p.
-\]
-Indeed, \(m\le p\), while
-\(\beta(1-1/q)\le p\); in the non-Hilbert regime
-\(\beta>2r\), both sides of the latter inequality equal
-\(2r\beta/(\beta+2r)\).  Since \(m+1>p\), the final inequality in
-\eqref{eq:all-order-stable-critical-remainder} also holds on the unit ball.
-
-Taylor's formula gives \eqref{eq:all-order-stable-integrated-remainder}
-before its norm assertion.  For fixed \(x\), the local estimate implies
-\[
- s^p\|F_\cdot^{(\alpha,d)}(x/s)
-       -T_m^{(\alpha,d)}(\cdot,x/s)\|_q\longrightarrow0,
-\]
-whereas \eqref{eq:all-order-stable-critical-remainder} bounds this expression
-by \(C|x|^p\).  Minkowski's inequality and dominated convergence prove the
-claimed \(L^q\) remainder.  Boundedness of the modes follows again from
-Proposition~\ref{prop:stable-kernel-input-package}.
-\end{proof}

-\begin{lemma}[Two-background critical Bregman transfer]
-\label{lem:two-background-critical-bregman-transfer}
-Let \(1<q\le2\), \(p\ge r>0\), and \(pq=2r\).  On a probability space
-\((E,\Omega)\), suppose \(g_s\ge c_s>0\),
-\[
- \int g_s\dd\Omega=1,\qquad c_s\longrightarrow1,
- \qquad \|g_s-1\|_{L^1(\Omega)}\longrightarrow0.
-\]
-Let \(B\in L^\infty(\Omega)\), and suppose
-\[
- v_s=s^{-r}B+o(s^{-r})\quad\hbox{in }L^\infty(\Omega),
- \qquad \|e_s\|_{L^q(\Omega)}=o(s^{-p}).
-\]
-If \(g_s+v_s+e_s\ge0\) and both \(g_s\Omega\) and
-\((g_s+v_s+e_s)\Omega\) are probability measures, then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-background-critical-bregman-transfer}
- D_{\rm KL}((g_s+v_s+e_s)\Omega\|g_s\Omega)
- =\frac{s^{-2r}}2\int B^2\dd\Omega+o(s^{-2r}).
-\end{equation}
-\end{lemma}
-
-The hypotheses on the denominator in this lemma deliberately stop short of
-\(L^\infty\)-convergence to one.  They require only a positive lower bound
-approaching one, mass normalization, and \(L^1\)-convergence.  This weaker
-interface is what permits a heavy-tailed translated mixture to serve as the
-background.
-
-\begin{proof}
-For \(g>0\), write \(\Psi_g(z)=g\Phi(z/g)\).  Scaling
-Lemma~\ref{lem:critical-lq-kl-perturbation} shows, whenever
-\(|v/g|\le1/4\) and \(g+v+e\ge0\), that
-\[
- 0\le\Psi_g(v+e)-\Psi_g(v)
-      -\log(1+v/g)e\le C_q g^{1-q}|e|^q.
-\]
-For large \(s\), the hypotheses give \(g_s\ge1/2\) and
-\(\|v_s/g_s\|_\infty\le1/4\).  Therefore H\"older's inequality yields
-\begin{align*}
- &\left|D_{\rm KL}((g_s+v_s+e_s)\Omega\|g_s\Omega)
-       -\int\Psi_{g_s}(v_s)\dd\Omega\right|\\
- &\qquad\le
- C\|v_s\|_{L^{q/(q-1)}}\|e_s\|_{L^q}
- +C\|e_s\|_{L^q}^q
- =o(s^{-r-p})+o(s^{-pq})=o(s^{-2r}).
-\end{align*}
-Uniform Taylor expansion at zero gives
-\[
- \int\Psi_{g_s}(v_s)\dd\Omega
- =\frac12\int\frac{v_s^2}{g_s}\dd\Omega+O(\|v_s\|_\infty^3).
-\]
-Finally,
-\[
- \left|\int B^2(g_s^{-1}-1)\dd\Omega\right|
- \le2\|B\|_\infty^2\|g_s-1\|_1\longrightarrow0,
-\]
-and \eqref{eq:two-background-critical-bregman-transfer} follows.
-\end{proof}

-\begin{lemma}[Finite-difference moment blocks]
-\label{lem:stable-finite-difference-blocks}
-Let \(r\ge1\), let \(e\) be a unit vector, and define
-\[
- \sigma_R:=2^{1-r}\sum_{k=0}^r(-1)^{r-k}\binom rk
-                 \delta_{(k+1)Re}=A_R^+-A_R^-.
-\]
-Then \(A_R^+\) and \(A_R^-\) are probability measures and
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-block-moment-identities}
- \int x^\gamma\dd\sigma_R(x)=0\quad(|\gamma|<r),
- \qquad
- \int(e\cdot x)^r\dd\sigma_R(x)=2^{1-r}r!R^r.
-\end{equation}
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-The positive and negative binomial coefficients each sum to \(2^{r-1}\),
-and the order-\(r\) forward-difference identity gives
-\eqref{eq:stable-block-moment-identities}.  In particular, when \(r=1\),
-\(\sigma_R=\delta_{2Re}-\delta_{Re}\); the same cancellation and nonzero
-first-difference conclusions hold without a separate construction.
-\end{proof}

-Put \(x_j=(r+1)R_je\), choose
-\(s_j=\kappa R_jw_j^{1/\beta}<R_j/4\), and set
-\(E_j=B(x_j,s_j)\).  There are constants \(a_r>0\) and
-\(C_{\alpha,d,r}<\infty\), independent of \(j,\kappa,R_j,w_j\), such that
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-moving-ball-probability-separation}
- (p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu)(E_j)\ge a_rw_j,

- \ge 2^{1-r}w_j\int_{B(0,1)}p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)\dd y

-opposite-sign atoms are at least \(R_j\) from \(x_j\).  Every earlier atom
-has norm at most \((r+1)R_{j-1}<R_j/4\), whereas every later atom has norm at
-least \(R_{j+1}>4(r+1)R_j\); the atom at zero obeys the earlier-atom bound.
-After subtracting the radius \(s_j<R_j/4\), every such atom \(z\) satisfies
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:stable-moving-ball-distance}
- \operatorname{dist}(z,E_j)\ge3R_j/4.
-\end{equation}
-For \(y\in E_j\), the stable density upper bound and scaling now give
-\[
- p_{s_j}^{(\alpha,d)}(y-z)
- \le C_{\alpha,d,r}s_j^\alpha R_j^{-\beta}.

\section{Auxiliary order-eight Laurent coefficient certificate}%
\label{app:order-eight-laurent-certificate}

This appendix gives the finite certificate for the order-eight rows used to
audit the \(A_8\) substitution.  The main coefficient hierarchy has already
been proved in Section~\ref{sec:entropy-asymptotics}; the material below is
a reproducible check of one explicit example.  The single convention is
\[
q_{n,k}=2^{-n}(-\ii)^n
For \(|z|\le1\), the local quotient--Taylor estimate
\eqref{eq:local-multidim-taylor-remainder} implies the first line of
\eqref{eq:critical-lq-global-remainder}.  For \(|z|>1\), the exact identity
gives \(\|F_\cdot(z)\|_{q_d}\le C_d|z|^{4/q_d}=C_d|z|^{p_d}\).
Every coefficient of \(T_m\) is bounded in \(y\), and \(m\le p_d\), so
\(\|T_m(\cdot,z)\|_{q_d}\le C_d|z|^{p_d}\).  Finally,
\(m+1>p_d\), which proves the last inequality for \(|z|\le1\).
\end{proof}
Corollary~\ref{thm:poisson-defect-amplification} states that equality in
\[
\mathcal E_8(\nu)\ge
\frac{13\sigma^2}{8}\Delta_6(\nu)
\]
holds if and only if $\nu_c=\rho_\sigma$.  Combining these equivalences
proves all the listed conditions equivalent.
\end{proof}

-This appendix separates the theorem statements in the paper from nearby
-results that use similar words--entropy, transport, Poisson, heat profile,
-or Hardy--Stein--for different objects.  The introduction organizes the
-closest comparisons by mathematical mechanism.  The longer table below
-records additional entropy, Sobolev--Bregman, heat-profile,
-Poisson-channel papers, Cauchy-divergence formulas, and general
-entropy-representation references.  The distinctions used in the table are
-structural: the present law \(\nu\) is fixed, the reference is the
-mean-matched harmonic Poisson/Cauchy kernel, and the coefficients are obtained
-by expanding the quotient before applying
-\(\Phi(s)=(1+s)\log(1+s)-s\).

-
-Closed formulas for divergences between Cauchy laws also do not imply the
-coefficient hierarchy above.  Results such as Nielsen--Okamura
-\cite{NielsenOkamura2023Cauchy}, Nielsen
-\cite{Nielsen2020CauchyVoronoi}, and Verd{\'u}
-\cite{Verdu2023Cauchy} evaluate \(f\)-divergences or information-geometric
-quantities when both arguments are members of a finite-dimensional Cauchy
-family.  In the present problem the numerator \(P_t*\nu\) is generally a
-mixture of Cauchy translates, not a single Cauchy law; only the denominator is
-the mean-matched Cauchy kernel.  Even when a law is approximated by a nearby
-Cauchy profile, the KL coefficients are not obtained by differentiating the
-two-parameter Cauchy divergence formula: after centering, the linear term in
-the quotient integrates to zero, while the \(t^{-2m}\) coefficient collects
-all products of quotient modes whose total order is \(2m\) through the
-nonlinear series for \(\Phi\).  The fixed-law hierarchy is therefore a
-moment-polynomial constant-term calculation for a Cauchy mixture quotient,
-not an expansion inside the Cauchy statistical manifold.
-
-The regularly varying boundary theorem uses Karamata theory in a different
-role from stable-limit entropy theory.  The integrated slow-variation facts
-and direct/tail integral theorems are classical
-\cite{BinghamGoldieTeugels1987RegularVariation}; they identify the truncated
-moment and control the local and far parts of the Cayley quotient.  Entropic
-convergence to stable laws and stable de Bruijn or fractional-information
-identities
-\cite{BobkovChistyakovGotze2013StableEntropy,Johnson2013StableDeBruijn,
-Toscani2016StableEntropy} instead concern normalized convolution sequences,
-stable interpolation, or entropy dissipation relative to a stable target.
-They do not give the coefficient-subtracted, moving-Cauchy-reference
-asymptotic of
-Theorem~\ref{cor:main-body-conditional-missing-top-moment-tail}.  The new
-step is the distribution-level \(L^\infty\cap L^1(\omega)\) quotient jet at
-the exact divergent moment boundary and its transfer to the signed
-\(t^{-2N}\ell_L(t)\) residual.  Karamata's theorem itself is cited as an
-external input and is not reproved here.
-
-The Poisson terminology also hides adjacent but different entropy theories.
-Poisson-channel papers such as Guo--Shamai--Verd{\'u}
-\cite{GuoShamaiVerdu2008PoissonChannel} and Atar--Weissman
-\cite{AtarWeissman2012PoissonChannel} study conditional count outputs
-\(Y|X\sim{\rm Poisson}(\gamma X)\) or continuous-time counting processes and
-relate mutual information, relative entropy, and estimation loss.  These are
-count-output models rather than harmonic smoothing by \(P_t\), so they do not
-produce the quotient expansion used in Theorems~\ref{thm:main-A}
-and~\ref{thm:main-B}.
-
-Small-time heat-kernel entropy expansions have a different limiting regime.
-For example, the expansions of
-Menkovski--Portegies--Ravelonanosy
-\cite{MenkovskiPortegiesRavelonanosy2024HeatKernelEntropy} treat the
-relative entropy between a heat kernel and normalized Riemannian volume as the
-heat time tends to zero; the coefficients are universal local geometric
-invariants of the underlying manifold.  By contrast, here \(t\to\infty\), the
-underlying space is Euclidean, the reference is the translated harmonic
-Poisson/Cauchy kernel \(P_t(\cdot-\bar\gamma)\), and the coefficients depend
-on the fixed input law only through its centred moments and the Cayley Laurent
-constant-term rule.  Process and discretization entropy asymptotics, such as
-Fageot--Fallah--Horel
-\cite{FageotFallahHorel2022EntropicCompressibilityLevy} and
-Ghourchian--Amini--Gohari
-\cite{GhourchianAminiGohari2018InnovationCompressibility}, concern
-compressibility or innovation limits rather than a single fixed law smoothed
-by a harmonic semigroup.  General representation formulas, including the
-Gibbs--Donsker--Varadhan variational formula
-\cite{DonskerVaradhan1975AsymptoticI,DupuisEllis1997WeakConvergence} and
-semigroup de Bruijn identities such as
-\cite{DeBruijn1953,HirataNemotoYoshida2012IntegralRepresentation,
-Yoshida2017RelativeEntropyDiffusion}, identify entropy through optimization
-or dissipation.  They are structural identities, not coefficient evaluations
-for the matched large-\(t\) functional in
-\eqref{eq:intro-main-functional}.
-
-\section{Fourth-moment coefficient-calculus example}%
-\label{app:optional-fourth-moment-coefficient-algebra}
-\label{app:fourth-moment-coupling-proof}
-
-The fourth-moment material is not used in the three main theorems.  Its role
-is only to illustrate how the sixth-order coefficient \(A_6\) can be read as
-a simple algebraic defect after normalizing to unit variance.  The proof
-below supplies the elementary coupling estimate underlying the
-fourth-moment discussion; it uses no finite-time KL estimate and no
-eighth-order coefficient.
-
-\begin{lemma}[Normalized fourth-moment defect algebra]%
-\label{lem:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-defect-algebra}
-Let \(X\) be a real random variable with \(\EE X=0\), \(\EE X^2=1\), and
-\(\EE X^4<\infty\).  Put
-\[
-\beta_3=\EE X^3,\qquad
-Q_2=X^2-1-\beta_3X,\qquad
-\kappa=\EE Q_2^2,\qquad
-\eta=\frac{\beta_3^2}{32}+\frac{\kappa}{8}.
-\]
-Then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-algebra}
-\eta
-=\frac{\beta_3^2}{32}+\frac{\EE(X^2-1-\beta_3X)^2}{8}
-=\frac{\EE X^4-1}{8}-\frac{3\beta_3^2}{32}.
-\end{equation}
-In particular \(\eta\ge0\), and \(\eta=0\) if and only if
-\(\mathcal L(X)=\rho_1:=\frac12(\delta_{-1}+\delta_1)\).
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Expanding \(Q_2^2\) and using \(\EE X=0\), \(\EE X^2=1\), and
-\(\EE X^3=\beta_3\) gives
-\[
-\kappa
-=\EE[(X^2-1-\beta_3X)^2]
-=\EE[(X^2-1)^2]-\beta_3^2
-=\EE X^4-1-\beta_3^2.
-\]
-Substitution gives \eqref{eq:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-algebra}.
-The first displayed form of \(\eta\) proves non-negativity.  If
-\(\eta=0\), then \(\beta_3=0\) and \(Q_2=0\) almost surely, hence
-\(X^2=1\) almost surely; since \(\EE X=0\), the two signs have equal mass.
-The converse is immediate.
-\end{proof}
-
-\begin{lemma}[Elementary normalized \(W_2\) coupling]%
-\label{lem:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-w2-coupling}
-Let \(X\) be a real random variable with \(\EE X=0\), \(\EE X^2=1\), and
-\(\EE X^4<\infty\), and define \(\eta\) as in
-Lemma~\ref{lem:appendix-normalized-fourth-moment-defect-algebra}.  Then
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:appendix-normalized-sign-rademacher-coupling}
-W_2(\mathcal L(X),\rho_1)
-\le 4\eta^{1/4}+8\eta^{1/2}.
-\end{equation}
-\end{lemma}
-
-\begin{proof}
-Let
-\[
-M:=\EE[(X^2-1)^2].
-\]
-The calculation in the preceding lemma gives
-\[
-M=\kappa+\beta_3^2\le32\eta .
-\]
-Let \(S=1\) on \(\{X\ge0\}\) and \(S=-1\) on \(\{X<0\}\), and write
-\(r_p=\mathcal L(S)=p\delta_1+(1-p)\delta_{-1}\).  For every real \(x\),
-with this convention at \(x=0\),
-\[
-|x-\operatorname{sgn}x|\le |x^2-1|.
-\]
-Indeed \(|x^2-1|=|x-1|(x+1)\) for \(x\ge0\), and
-\(|x^2-1|=|x+1|(1-x)\) for \(x<0\).  Coupling \(X\) and \(S\) on the same
-probability space gives
-\begin{equation}\label{eq:appendix-couple-x-to-sign}
-W_2(\mathcal L(X),r_p)
-\le \bigl(\EE|X-S|^2\bigr)^{1/2}
-\le M^{1/2}.
-\end{equation}
-
-It remains to couple the biased sign law to the symmetric Rademacher law.
-On the two-point set \(\{-1,1\}\), optimal quadratic transport moves the
-excess mass \(|p-\frac12|\) across distance \(2\), so
-\[
-W_2(r_p,\rho_1)^2=4\left|p-\frac12\right|.
-\]
-Since \(\EE X=0\),
-\[
-2p-1=\EE S=\EE(S-X),
-\]
-and Cauchy--Schwarz together with
-\eqref{eq:appendix-couple-x-to-sign} gives
-\[
-\left|p-\frac12\right|
-\le \frac12\EE|S-X|
-\le \frac12 M^{1/2}.
-\]
-Consequently
-\[
-W_2(r_p,\rho_1)\le \sqrt2\,M^{1/4}.
-\]
-The triangle inequality now yields
-\[
-W_2(\mathcal L(X),\rho_1)
-\le M^{1/2}+\sqrt2\,M^{1/4}
-\le \sqrt{32}\,\eta^{1/2}+\sqrt2\,32^{1/4}\eta^{1/4}.
-\]
-Since \(\sqrt{32}<8\) and \(\sqrt2\,32^{1/4}=2^{7/4}<4\), this proves
-\eqref{eq:appendix-normalized-sign-rademacher-coupling}.
-\end{proof}
-
-For a law \(\nu\) with mean \(\bar\gamma\) and variance \(\sigma^2>0\), set
-\(X=(\gamma-\bar\gamma)/\sigma\), let
-\(\nu_c=(\gamma-\bar\gamma)_\#\nu\), and put
-\(\rho_\sigma=\frac12(\delta_{-\sigma}+\delta_\sigma)\).  Quadratic
-Wasserstein distance is homogeneous under dilation:
-\[
-W_2\bigl((x\mapsto ax)_\#\mu,(x\mapsto ax)_\#\rho\bigr)
-=|a|\,W_2(\mu,\rho).
-\]
-Define
-\[
-\Delta_6(\nu)
-:=\sigma^6\left(
-\frac{\beta_3^2}{32}+\frac{\EE(X^2-1-\beta_3X)^2}{8}
-\right).
-\]
-Combining this dilation identity with the normalized lemma gives exactly the
-estimate used in the main text,
-\[
-W_2(\nu_c,\rho_\sigma)
-\le
-4\,\sigma^{-1/2}\Delta_6(\nu)^{1/4}
-+8\,\sigma^{-2}\Delta_6(\nu)^{1/2},
-\]
-Equality \(\Delta_6(\nu)=0\) is equivalent to the symmetric two-point centred
-law.  Thus the appendix supplies a self-contained algebraic coupling proof,
-not an additional finite-time stability theorem.
-
-\section{Weighted trigonometric normalization}%
-\label{app:entropy-integrals}
-\label{app:background-symbol-criterion}
-
-This appendix records the change of variables behind the Laurent coefficient
-normalization.  Set \(y=\tan\theta\),
-\(-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2\).  Then
-\[
-  \frac{\dd y}{\pi(1+y^2)}=\frac{\dd\theta}{\pi}.
-\]
-With \(z=e^{2\ii\theta}\),
-\[
-  \cos(2k\theta)=\frac{z^k+z^{-k}}2,\qquad
-  \sin(2k\theta)=\frac{z^k-z^{-k}}{2\ii}.
-\]
-Thus the Cauchy mode integrals in
-Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-fourier-mode-integral-algorithm} are exactly Haar
-constant terms:
-\[
-  \int_{\RR}\prod_j u_{n_j}(y)\,\omega(\dd y)
-  =[z^0]\prod_j Q_{n_j}(z).
-\]
-For order eight, Appendix~\ref{app:order-eight-laurent-certificate} records
-the row certificate as a finite coefficient-calculus check.
-
-\fi
